conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the surgical team. You're here because of recurrent pancreatitis and a cyst in the tail of your pancreas. We’re planning to do a distal pancreatectomy and remove the spleen today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, yes, I’ve been having a lot of left-sided pain. Is the surgery definitely needed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ve had multiple episodes of pancreatitis with no clear cause. Imaging shows the body and tail of the pancreas are enlarged, and the pain is centered there. Removing that part should help prevent future attacks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the spleen too? Why?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because the blood supply to the spleen comes from the same artery that runs through the tail of the pancreas. It’s safer to remove it during this surgery to avoid complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m also worried about my digestion. I’ve had malabsorption for a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s why we’re also doing a small bowel biopsy. We’ll take a small sample to check if there’s any underlying issue causing the malabsorption.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need lifelong supplements after this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Since part of the pancreas is being removed, you may need pancreatic enzyme supplements. We’ll monitor that closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my anemia? That’s been a problem too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your hemoglobin is low. We’ll keep an eye on it. The surgery team will be cautious due to your Von Willebrand’s disease, which affects clotting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m also allergic to morphine. I get really nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Noted. We’ll use alternative pain medications. You’ll have a PCA pump initially, but not with morphine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, we just got back from surgery. The distal pancreatectomy and splenectomy went well. We also did the small bowel biopsy. You’re in recovery now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How do I feel? I’m groggy but okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal. You’ll be on IV fluids and pain meds. You’re not allowed to eat yet—NPO—until your bowels wake up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will that take?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Usually a few days. We’ll start with clear liquids once you pass gas and your abdomen isn’t bloated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your NG tube was removed this morning. That’s a good sign—your stomach is starting to work again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That feels better. Can I drink water?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We’ll wait until you have bowel sounds and some flatus. Maybe tomorrow for sips.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. WBC was high yesterday but is coming down. That’s expected after surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the infection risk higher without a spleen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, long-term. You’ll need vaccines and to be careful with fevers. But for now, you’re on antibiotics just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—you passed gas and your abdomen is soft. We’re going to start you on clear liquids today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have apple juice?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, small amounts. We’ll watch for nausea or bloating. If you tolerate it, we’ll advance your diet slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Your pain is better, and you’re on oral pain meds now. We’re switching from the PCA pump.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still need a higher dose than usual, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ve always needed more. We’re using a combination to keep you comfortable without over-sedation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the biopsy results?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The small bowel biopsy came back normal. No signs of celiac or other malabsorption causes. That’s good—we can focus on pancreatic support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your JP drain amylase was checked yesterday—117. That’s a bit elevated, but not concerning. We’ll remove the drain today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What does that number mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It checks for pancreatic fluid leak. A high level could mean a leak, but yours isn’t high enough to worry. You’re healing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pancreas tissue they removed—was there pancreatitis or a cyst?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Actually, no. The pathology report says the tissue looked normal—no cyst, no signs of chronic pancreatitis. But that doesn’t mean the surgery wasn’t needed. Sometimes damage isn’t visible under the microscope.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why did I keep having attacks?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t know for sure. It could be functional or due to subtle structural issues. But since your pain was localized there, removing it was the best option.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling a bit dizzy when I sit up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely your orthostatic hypotension. You have a history of that. We’re monitoring your blood pressure and restarted your fludrocortisone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart racing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also part of your condition. You have tachycardia syndrome. As long as you’re not symptomatic, it’s okay. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. You’ve had a bowel movement, you’re on a regular diet, and your incision looks clean. We’re discharging you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy for a few weeks. No heavy lifting. Keep the steri strips on until they fall off. Watch for fever, redness, or drainage from the incision.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue your amitriptyline and fludrocortisone. We’ll start pancreatic enzymes if you have diarrhea or bloating. Follow up with surgery and gastroenterology in two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the spleen—what about infections?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—get the pneumococcal, meningococcal, and Hib vaccines if you haven’t already. Always tell doctors you don’t have a spleen if you get sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel hopeful this will help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We do too. You’ve been through a lot, but you’re on the mend. We’ll see you soon in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—my Sicca syndrome. Should I keep using eye drops?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue artificial tears and stay hydrated. It’s unrelated to the surgery but important for comfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my iron? My levels are always low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll check your hemoglobin at your follow-up. You may need iron supplements, especially after surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll watch for fatigue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good idea. Call us if you feel weak or short of breath. Otherwise, rest and recover.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re glad you’re feeling better. Discharge papers will be ready soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I drive in a few days?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not for at least two weeks. Wait until you’re off strong pain meds and can move comfortably.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll have my mom help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good plan. Take it one day at a time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m just glad the pain is gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We are too. That’s the best sign that this was the right step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Get some rest and we’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.
